common_name: Col de Dame Grise Fig (Grey Neck of the Lady Fig)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; give Col de Dame Grise a long warm season since it ripens later than most Gulf Coast figs and skips the early breba crop entirely.

directions: This French heirloom is one of the gray-skinned members of the historic Col de Dame family, distinct from the pale Col de Dame Blanc and near-black Col de Dame Noir. Fruit is medium-to-large and pear-shaped with thick greenish-purple skin that develops a grayish bloom and fine surface cracking at full ripeness, surrounding dense, dark red, jam-textured flesh. Unlike many dual-cropping figs, it produces only a single late main crop with no breba, so patience is rewarded with an unusually rich, wine-like sweetness in early fall. The tree is a vigorous, heavy-cropping grower once established.

common_name: Bourjasotte Noire Fig (Noire de Barbentane, Black Bourjasotte)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; thicker, less rain-sensitive skin makes it a reasonable option for humid Gulf Coast summers where thinner-skinned black figs tend to split.

directions: Grown around the western Mediterranean for centuries under names like Brogiotto Nero and Noire de Barbentane, this dark purple-to-black fig is a separate old cultivar from the paler Bourjassotte Grise. Fruit is large and broad-based with a blue-purple bloom over near-black skin, enclosing dense, glossy dark red flesh with a honeyed, faintly tart, berry-and-melon flavor. Its notably firm, thicker skin gives it better resistance to rain-cracking and splitting than many other dark-fleshed figs of similar quality. Expect a single generous main crop rather than a significant breba flush.

common_name: Adriatic JH Fig (JH Adriatic, Joe Hood Selection)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; this Austin, Texas-sourced selection has performed reliably in hot Gulf South summers where some older Adriatic clones in commerce have declined from virus buildup.

directions: Adriatic JH is a named selection maintained by Texas fig grower Joe Hood of Austin, distinct from White Adriatic and reportedly healthier and more productive than some virus-affected Adriatic clones circulating in the nursery trade. Fruit ripens later in the season than typical White Adriatic and is medium-sized with pale green skin and deep red pulp, with a berry-forward flavor. It bears a modest breba crop followed by a heavier main crop, and its Texas origin and heat tolerance make it a reasonable candidate for Gulf Coast dooryards.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; long maintained among South Louisiana households and needs no special care beyond typical Gulf Coast fig culture.

directions: Smith is a heirloom fig long maintained in the Becnel family of Plaquemines Parish, Louisiana, and later used briefly as breeding stock in fig improvement work in Louisiana. Fruit is large and somewhat flattened, yellow skin blushed with brown, opening to deep red flesh with a distinctive drop of honey at the eye and outstanding sweetness. The cold-hardier reselection sold as Texas BA-1 traces back to this same variety and is a good option where Smith itself proves less reliable through winter. Like most Southern heirloom figs it is self-fertile, easy-care, and productive with minimal attention once established.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; the early ripening breba crop can beat Gulf Coast summer heat and disease pressure that affects later-fruiting cultivars.

directions: Paradiso is an old Neapolitan variety recorded in early-19th-century Italian pomological literature and long grown around the Mediterranean under regional names such as Brogiotto and Albero d'Oro. It is an early-ripening, two-crop fig with green-to-yellow skin and dark red pulp carrying an intense strawberry-berry sweetness. Because the name was widely reused by different growers over the centuries, several distinct strains circulate in today's collector trade under different labels, so expect some variation between sources. Even accounting for that uncertainty, well-sourced Paradiso trees are consistently praised for rich flavor and reliable early cropping.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in late winter to spring in well-drained soil in full sun; cold hardiness and split resistance make it a reasonable choice for occasional Gulf Coast cold snaps and humid ripening seasons.

directions: Battaglia Green traces to cuttings an Italian immigrant family brought to Virginia Beach, Virginia, where it was propagated and named by grower Sandy Battaglia; it is an Adriatic-type fig, distinct from both White Adriatic and Adriatic JH. Medium-sized fruit keeps its bright green skin even at full ripeness, hiding a jammy, strawberry-red interior with an intensely fruity flavor. It is notably cold-hardy and early-ripening, producing both a breba and a main crop, and shows good resistance to splitting in humid weather even though it prefers a drier climate overall.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in late winter to spring in well-drained soil in full sun; ability to fruit on new shoots after a freeze-back makes it useful insurance for the rare hard-freeze winter in zone 9a.

directions: Michurinska-10 originated near the town of Michurin on Bulgaria's Black Sea coast and is grown chiefly for exceptional cold hardiness among quality-fruited figs. Fruit is medium-sized with a bright, sweet, berry-toned flavor, produced as an early breba crop followed by a main crop. Its key advantage over most Gulf South cultivars is that it reliably sets a main crop even on new growth pushed after a hard freeze kills the top of the tree back to the ground, so a single unusually cold winter is far less likely to cost a full year's harvest. Because it was selected for far colder climates than the Gulf Coast, treat its heat and humidity tolerance here as unproven rather than assumed.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; self-fertile and parthenocarpic like other common figs, setting fruit without any pollinator or fig wasp.

directions: An old, robust and productive French fig traced to the collection of grower M. Baud, Grise de Saint-Jean is distinct from the other gray-skinned figs in the collection such as Bourjassotte Grise and Col de Dame Grise. Fruit is large and pear-shaped with thin, hazy gray-purple-and-green skin and pinkish-brown flesh that often has a pool of honey at the eye. It is a two-crop variety whose breba flush is especially well regarded, since it can ripen reliably even in seasons too cool or short for the late main crop to fully mature. Vigorous and productive once established, it needs the same easy care as any common fig.

common_name: Deanna Fig (UC Davis Cold-Hardy Large-Fruited Fig)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in late winter to spring in well-drained soil in full sun; large fruit size and crack resistance benefit from consistent moisture through ripening, which the humid Gulf Coast summer usually provides.

directions: Deanna was developed through University of California, Davis fig breeding work as a cold-hardier, crack-resistant alternative to Calimyrna-type figs, which need caprification and are prone to splitting. Fruit is exceptionally large, often exceeding 100 grams, with green-yellow skin that ripens toward yellow and sweet amber-to-strawberry flesh with a pronounced honey flavor. It bears a substantial breba crop in addition to a significant main crop and tolerates winter cold well beyond what most Gulf Coast winters require, giving a wide safety margin against the occasional hard freeze.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; reported to perform especially well in hot, humid climates, making it a promising light-skinned fig for Gulf Coast dooryards.

directions: White Triana is an old-world Spanish heirloom associated with the Triana district of Seville in Andalusia, distinct from the White Adriatic, White Genoa, and White Marseilles already grown here. Fruit is medium-sized, ripening to a pale yellow-green-to-creamy-gold skin with translucent amber, lightly strawberry-tinged flesh that carries a syrupy, low-acid sweetness. It is self-fruitful and produces both a breba and a main crop, and growers report it holds up especially well through long, hot, humid summers rather than favoring the drier Mediterranean climates that stress some other Spanish and Italian heirlooms.
